title: Why is the bias factor not an event weight?
question: 为什么不能将生成事件数直接除以 bias factor？
source: X. Zhu, Y. Zhang, Biasing study, 25 Jun. 2024, pp. 3–5, 14.
answer: We scale the rare-process cross section by a bias factor b. The probability of that process happening also depends on competing interactions and the distance available in the material. This 1-dimensional model assumes constant effective cross sections along that distance. We fit the scan and evaluate the probability at b = 1. The pool is the set of eligible particles above the bias-energy cut. The pool fraction then converts the conditional probability into a rate per incident particle. This rate-calibration method is separate from generic transport-weight bookkeeping.

title: Which events enter the biasing normalisation?
question: Ntotal、Npool、Nrare 和最终存储事件数有什么区别？
source: Biasing study, pp. 4–5, 11, 15. Historical study counters.
answer: We count incident events, eligible events and rare interactions separately. Only some rare events pass the output filters. In this study, we allow at most 1 biased interaction per event and record the counters in truth_cutflow. We fit the rare-to-pool ratio before interpreting the final-state acceptance. A fit made after a truth trigger describes a conditional selected sample, so it cannot simply be read as the unfiltered process rate.

title: Does the finite target thickness matter?
question: 靶很薄，截面比是否等于发生概率？为什么 target 和 ECAL 不一样？
source: Biasing study, pp. 6–7; original plots retained.
answer: These are the original GMM (photon conversion to a muon pair) scans from the 2024 study. The upper panels show the rare-to-pool probability and the lower panels show the simulation-to-fit ratio. In the target, an eligible photon can escape before interacting. In the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter), it has more material to cross. This explains why a branching-ratio approximation works differently in the 2 regions. The displayed fit parameters and uncertainties belong to this historical configuration; they are not the positron-campaign calibration.

title: What does the photonuclear scan test?
question: 如何检查 biasing 没有改变物理？这些拟合证明了什么？
source: Biasing study, pp. 6–7; original plots retained.
answer: PN (photonuclear) interactions show the same rise and saturation. We compare the conditional interaction probability across the bias scan with the fitted model. Agreement here does not by itself validate all secondary-particle spectra or the final background tail. We also compare dedicated samples with inclusive production where there are enough events. The rates on these plots belong to the 2024 study and are not substituted for the positron sample normalisations.

title: How well did the early rate comparison agree?
question: biasing 和 inclusive 的一致性能达到什么程度？
source: Biasing study, p. 9. Values rounded from the original rate table.
answer: The original rate table is useful because it also shows the discrepancies. GMM (photon conversion to a muon pair), PN (photonuclear) and EN (electronuclear) rates were compared with an inclusive sample of about 10⁷ events. Some ratios differ substantially from 1. A zero observed count in the rarest sample does not measure a zero rate. We do not turn these historical ratios into a systematic uncertainty for the later positron campaign. The campaign uses its own normalisation and inclusive checks, shown in the main report and the other backups.

title: How is a biased sample normalised to POT?
question: 给一个带数值的 effective POT 和归一化例子？
source: X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900; campaign normalisation table.
answer: For PN (photonuclear) production in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter), the campaign convention gives 1.48 × 10¹¹ effective POT (Positrons On Target). We obtain it from 10⁸ generation attempts, an acceptance of 0.2738 and a process branching ratio of 1.85 × 10⁻⁴. The 3 × 10¹⁴ POT benchmark is about 2,030 times this effective POT. The POT normalisation factor scales the selected prediction. It does not recover a tail from a sample with no surviving events, and it is not the cross-section bias factor. The full process table is on backup 3.

title: Does zero survival prove a background-free search?
question: 最终 cutflow 全是 0，为什么还要外推？零存活能给什么上限？
source: Campaign POT: arXiv:2609.05900. Poisson illustration calculated here.
answer: No surviving simulated event is not enough to claim a background-free search. As a simple counting illustration, 0 observed events corresponds to an upper Poisson mean of 2.30 at 90% confidence. Scaling from 2.5 × 10⁹ to 3 × 10¹⁴ POT gives a very weak bound of about 2.76 × 10⁵ events. This calculation assumes an ideal unweighted Poisson sample with known equivalent POT. It is not a substitute for the profile-likelihood construction or a bound to apply blindly to weighted samples. It explains why the study uses sideband extrapolation for its nominal prediction.

title: Can the production filters remove useful events?
question: generator-level filter 是否会偏置最终 selection 或漏掉 signal-like events？
source: Positron production filters and fixed region definitions, arXiv:2609.05900.
answer: The production energy and momentum cuts are looser than the final analysis cuts. That is useful, but it is not by itself a proof that the filters have no effect. A truth quantity can differ from its reconstructed counterpart, and the 0-track categories need their own bookkeeping. We check the actual production definitions and the response near the boundaries. We also keep the filter acceptance with the sample. Any excluded phase space is absent from the prediction and cannot be recovered by reweighting.

title: Why is the gain concentrated near 90 MeV?
question: 为什么 90 MeV 特别好？为什么不是共振过程单独主导？
source: X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900; 2-body kinematics.
answer: For an 8 GeV positron and an electron at rest, the centre-of-mass energy is about 90.4 MeV. The photon energy in the centre-of-mass frame tends to 0 as the mediator mass approaches this value. This helps non-resonant annihilation pass a low-visible-energy selection. The detector-level efficiencies still determine the accepted yield. Bound-electron motion changes the ideal stationary-electron picture; the specific implementation should be checked against the production configuration rather than inferred from the illustration.

title: Do nuclei and electrons have the same luminosity?
question: 产生截面如何变成最终 signal yield？Z 因子有没有重复计算？
source: Dissertation target-luminosity and response-matrix definitions; arXiv:2609.05900.
answer: We use the number of scattering centres per unit target area. Nuclear bremsstrahlung uses nuclei; annihilation uses atomic electrons. For the same foil, the electron areal density is Z times the nuclear one. We include this factor once, according to how the cross section is defined. We then multiply the rate by the invisible branching fraction and the channel-to-region efficiency. The 10⁵ generated events per mass point determine that efficiency, not the physical event count. Electron-versus-positron comparisons use the same beam count and target. No running-year conversion is needed.

title: What supports the 1 MeV cell thresholds?
question: 1 MeV veto 是否现实？电子学噪声、pileup、通道数的影响在哪里？
source: DarkSHINE calorimeter design/readout studies; positron-analysis response assumptions.
answer: The ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) high-gain model gives an equivalent electronic noise of about 2.7 keV per channel. That provides context for a 1 MeV cut, but it does not determine the full probability of a noise-induced veto across many channels. The HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) threshold is an assumed performance in this campaign, which does not include complete noise and pileup digitisation. We would test the thresholds with prototype data and propagate the measured response into signal efficiency and background rejection.

title: When does the signal scale with epsilon squared?
question: 为什么用一个 signal strength？暗耦合、branching ratio 或模型变了怎么办？
source: Vector-portal benchmark and thermal-target definition, arXiv:2609.05900.
answer: At fixed mass and with the invisible branching fraction close to 1, the benchmark production rates scale approximately with epsilon squared. We can therefore use a common signal-strength parameter. For the thermal comparison, we choose alpha D = 0.5 and a mediator-to-dark-matter mass ratio of 3, which gives y equal to epsilon squared divided by 162. These are benchmark assumptions. A change in the decay branching fraction or lifetime can change the visible signature and the acceptance. A separate off-shell model should not be inferred from the on-shell efficiency samples.

title: Can the software speed-up factors be multiplied?
question: 软件总共快了多少倍？不同 benchmark 可以相乘吗？
source: DSS_716, pp. 7, 11, 13, 15; optical study by Qibin Liu.
answer: We quote these benchmarks separately because they measure different costs and use different configurations. Geometry navigation changes the transport time per event. Event-record optimisation changes storage. Filtering changes the number of costly events that we finish and write. The thread comparison uses 8 execution units on both sides, so it does not measure scaling from 1 core. The optical result compares full tracking with a lookup table. We can assess the total production cost only with an end-to-end benchmark under a common setup.

title: CalcHEP inputs and detector production
question: CalcHEP 到底生成了什么过程？束流、耦合和生成 cuts 怎么设？
source: Read-only bl0 configuration snapshots, 9 Nov. 2026; see sources/calchep.
answer: I can show the archived batch settings and the corresponding output headers. We found 8 GeV bremsstrahlung and radiative-annihilation batches requesting 10⁵ events. The calcHEP directory also has an 8 GeV multi-process batch containing a dark-matter-pair process, but it requests only 10 events. The diagramC example is a 4 GeV test. These records verify what those files specify. For detector production, we use the baseline 1, 8 GeV configurations in condor-script. The next page shows how each signal channel enters transport.

title: How does the signal enter detector transport?
question: 最终 detector transport 如何处理共振信号？
source: bl0 job/configuration and implementation snapshots; sources/calchep/README.md
answer: I can show an independent 8 GeV job configuration for the resonant channel at 60 MeV. It enables the resonant process, disables the LUT (Lookup Table), and disables visible decay. In the available transport implementation, we create an invisible dark photon along the incoming direction and terminate the positron. Although the class contains a lookup-table reader, the final-state function does not call it. The bremsstrahlung and radiative-annihilation templates use separate 8 GeV tables. The production configurations are stored in condor-script. The CalcHEP rate-test batches and the detector transport have different roles.
